Chapter 10 · Birth of the discipline · 1875–1910

Laboratories and experimental psychology

Leipzig, Harvard, Baltimore, Madrid and Tokyo: how psychology gained its own rooms, instruments, journals and students.

In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt began using a room at the University of Leipzig for psychological research with students. Textbooks repeat that date as the birth of scientific psychology. It is a useful milestone, but it is best read for what it was: one step within a broader process involving many people and places.

What were people trying to understand?

Wundt wanted to describe the elements of conscious experience (sensations, feelings) and how they combine. For him, experimental psychology was suited to the most elementary processes; complex phenomena such as language, myths and customs required another approach, which he developed in the ten volumes of his Völkerpsychologie (1900–1920).

With what methods?

The laboratory combined instruments from physiology (chronoscopes measuring thousandths of a second, metronomes, tachistoscopes) with trained observers who described their experience under tightly controlled conditions. This "experimental introspection" was not free reflection: short, immediate reports were requested and repeated many times.

Who took part?

Hundreds of students from many countries passed through Leipzig. Among them were James McKeen Cattell, who took the study of individual differences to the United States; Edward Titchener, who founded his own version, structuralism, at Cornell; and Emil Kraepelin, who applied experimental methods to psychiatry.

Meanwhile, William James had set up a demonstration room at Harvard around 1875. G. Stanley Hall opened a laboratory at Johns Hopkins in 1883, founded the American Journal of Psychology in 1887 and was the first president of the American Psychological Association (1892). In Spain, Luis Simarro held the first chair of experimental psychology at the Central University of Madrid from 1902. In Japan, Yūjirō Motora, who earned his doctorate at Johns Hopkins in 1888, promoted the discipline from Tokyo.

What did it contribute?

  • A place of its own: rooms, budget, instruments and a research routine.
  • Specialised journals, such as Philosophische Studien, founded by Wundt in 1881.
  • Training researchers who went on to open their own laboratories.
  • An academic identity distinct from philosophy and physiology, though closely linked to both.

What was revised later?

Introspective reports from different laboratories did not always agree. In Würzburg, Oswald Külpe's group argued for "imageless thought", which Titchener denied, and there was no clear way to settle the disagreement. That difficulty was one of behaviourism's arguments for abandoning introspection. Historians today also stress that the image of Wundt as a "pure introspectionist" is a simplification: his work was much broader, and part of it reached the English-speaking world through intermediaries who reinterpreted it.

The history of laboratories is also a history of exclusion: many women worked in them without being allowed degrees or posts. We tell that story in the profiles of Mary Whiton Calkins and Margaret Floy Washburn.
